The Restoration of a Lost Technique

By A Critic

The film opens on a shot nobody has been able to explain, and the explanation turns out to be older than the people who made it. What follows is an account of how a technique that had gone out of use came back, and of the three months it took to work out how it had ever been done in the first place.

The designers began where anyone begins, which is to say by reading everything written on the subject and discovering that almost nothing was. Two books, both out of print. A handful of interviews conducted decades after the fact by people who had not thought to ask the questions that mattered. The rest was inference.

So they guessed, and then they tested the guesses. The first attempts were too even: the light fell across the painted surface the way light falls on a wall, which is exactly what the technique is supposed to prevent. The trick, they eventually decided, was that the original painters had been working around a limitation rather than towards an effect.

Once that was understood the rest went quickly, which is the usual shape of these stories and no less true for being usual.

Related: Everything we know about the sequel

What is striking, watching the finished film, is how little of this shows. The shots look like the ones they were modelled on, which is the whole point and also the reason nobody will notice. That is the bargain of restoration work: succeed completely and the evidence of the work disappears along with the problem.

The director, asked about the expense, gave the answer directors give. It was worth it because it was worth it. In this case the footage makes the argument better than the sentence does.
